2. The case of the petitioner in brief is as under:
a.

The petitioner is the legally wedded wife of the first respondent, and their marriage solemnized on June 19, 2005, at Siddalingeshwara Temple in Yediyur, Kunigal Taluk,
Tumkur District, according to Hindu rites and customs.
They have one male child from this marriage.
The petitioner asserts that, a few months into the marriage, she became aware of the first respondent's true nature.
He has a habit of consuming alcohol and engaging in various vices, including an extramarital affair with a woman named Saraswathi, with whom he has a child named Rohith.
The first respondent frequently instigates Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT quarrels with the petitioner without cause, and the second and third respondents support him, often verbally abusing her.
When the petitioner confronted the first respondent about his affair, he subjected her to both mental and physical harassment.
Despite enduring this abuse with the hope that he would change, the first respondent continued his illicit relationship, neglecting his responsibilities towards the petitioner and their child.
On May 15, 2016, he drove the petitioner and their child from their home, after which they have been living with her parents in Bengaluru.

sentences.text: The petitioner has filed a police complaint against the respondents.
The Hulimavu Police registered a case under Crime No. 317/2016, invoking Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act.
A charge sheet has been filed against the respondents in the 5 th ACMM Court in Bengaluru under C.C. No. 27517/2016, which is currently pending consideration.
Despite several panchayat meetings and the advice of community elders, no resolution has been reached.
The first respondent operates a real estate and Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT travel agency named "Bhagavati Tours and Travels" and engages in automobile sales and purchases.
He owns two TATA Sumo vehicles and a goods vehicle, indicating a sufficient monthly income exceeding Rs. 1,00,000.

Therefore,
the petitioner prayed that the petition be allowed.
3. Following the service of notice, the respondents appeared in court through their Counsel.
Respondent No. 1 submitted a detailed objection to the main petition.
The remaining respondents subsequently filed a memorandum indicating that they were adopting the objections put forth by Respondent No. 1 as their own in relation to the main petition.
4. The contents of objections of respondents are as follows:
The respondent contends that there is no valid cause of action or actionable claim for domestic violence on the part of the petitioner.
The petitioner frequently suspects the character of the first respondent and engages in unnecessary quarrels without valid reasons.
She has failed to fulfil her duties as a wife, and her harassment toward the first respondent has Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT increased over time.
The first respondent has tolerated this behaviour for the sake of his family and child.
Despite his requests for the petitioner to mend her attitude, she remains adamant and has threatened to file false dowry complaints, aiming to put the first respondent and his parents behind bars.
The petitioner voluntarily deserted the first respondent, taking her belongings, including gold articles gifted by him, when she left the matrimonial home.
The first respondent has made several attempts to bring the petitioner and their child back home, but she has refused.
In further attempts to harass him, she filed a dowry harassment complaint against him and his family members.

Additionally, she has initiated a divorce petition in MC No. 2678/2016 before the Family Court in Bengaluru, based on false allegations intended to separate from the first respondent and to cause him mental and financial distress.
The petitioner operates a business supplying manpower to apartments, earning a substantial income.
She also owns residential properties that generate rental income.
With these contentions, the respondent prayed to reject the petition.
Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 5.

The respondent No.1 has deposed as RW.1 and produced the documents at Ex.R.1 to Ex.R.3 and closed his side.

She contended that, her marriage was solemnized with respondent No.1 on 19.06.2005 at Siddalingeshwara Temple,
Yediyur, Kunigal Taluk, Tumkur District., according to Hindu rites and customs.
Out of their wedlock, they have begotten a male child.
During the stay of petitioner in the house of respondents have given ill-treatment to the petitioner and drove out the petitioner without providing any maintenance.

11. The petitioner averred in the petition about the ill treatment and domestic violence committed by the respondents Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT and also deposed as Pw.1 by reiterating the petition averments and got marked documents at Ex.P.1 to P.10.
Pw.1 deposed about the ill-treatment given by the respondents while residing with him in the shared household.

The petitioner has produced the Ex.P.1 is the Photos along with C.D, Ex.P.2 is the School Fee paid Manjula M vs Ramachandra on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93755606/

Ex.P.10 is the Photo.
12.

The respondents in order to establish their defense, the respondent No.1 himself got examined as RW-1 by filing affidavit evidence in lieu of his examination in chief, wherein he has deposed in consonance with the averments of the objection and in support of his oral evidence he has got marked Ex.R.1 to Ex.R.3.

Ex.R.1 is the Certified copy of FIR, complaint and charge sheet in C.C.No.26099/2019, Ex.R.2 is the Certified copy of petition in M.C.No.2679/2019 and Ex.R.3 is the Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT Certified copy of Memorandum of petition and I.A in M.C.No.2678/2016.

13. The petitioner's primary grievance is that, a few months after their marriage, she discovered that the first respondent was engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman named Saraswathi,
resulting in the birth of a male child named Rohit.
When the petitioner confronted the first respondent about this matter, he, along with the other respondents, began to harass her, subjecting her to domestic violence.
Despite the petitioner's repeated requests for the first respondent to end his extramarital relationship, her pleas fell on deaf ears, and she continued to face harassment from the respondents.
Consequently, feeling she had no other option, the petitioner left the matrimonial home with her son and took refuge at her parental home.

14. On the other hand, the respondents deny the allegations regarding the first respondent's extramarital affair with Saraswathi and the claim that they have a son named Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT Rohit.
They assert that the petitioner tends to suspect the first respondent's character and has made numerous false accusations against him.

Furthermore, the respondents contend that the petitioner has filed a divorce petition against the first respondent in M.C. No. 2678/2016 before the Hon'ble Family Court in Bengaluru, based on unfounded allegations, with the sole intention of separating from him and harassing him.

15. The learned counsel representing the petitioner argued that, during the course of the marriage,
the first respondent engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman named Saraswathi, resulting in the birth of a child named Rohit.
The counsel presented Ex.P.8, the birth certificate of Rohit, as evidence that he is indeed the son of the first respondent and Saraswathi.
It was noted that the residential address listed on Ex.P.8 matches both the address in the petition's title and the address provided in the chief examination of the first respondent.
Therefore, the petitioner has clearly established that Rohit is the son of the first Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT respondent through Saraswathi.

The counsel argued that having a child with another woman while still married to the petitioner constitutes mental cruelty, which falls under Section 3 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.

sentences.text: Based on these arguments, the counsel requested that the court grant the relief sought by the petitioner.

16. In contrast, the counsel for the respondents vehemently argued that the allegations made by the petitioner regarding the first respondent's extramarital affair with a woman named Saraswathi, as Manjula M vs Ramachandra on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93755606/
4 well as the subsequent birth of their child, Rohit, are entirely false.

sentences.text: The counsel emphasized that the first respondent has consistently denied the authenticity of Ex.P.8, which is the birth certificate presented by the petitioner as evidence of Rohit's paternity.
During cross- examination, the first respondent refuted the claims associated with Ex.P.8, asserting that it does not accurately reflect the facts.
Furthermore, the counsel pointed out that the petitioner failed to produce the author of Ex.P.8 as a witness to authenticate the document.
The absence of this crucial Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT testimony raises significant doubts about the validity of the evidence presented.
As a result, the counsel contended that, Ex.P.8 should be deemed inadmissible in court.
Without this piece of evidence, they argued, the entire foundation of the petitioner's claims crumbles.
The counsel insisted that the allegations of an extramarital affair and the subsequent mental cruelty alleged by the petitioner lack credible substantiation.
Given the lack of admissible evidence to support the petitioner's allegations, the counsel urged the court to view the claims as unfounded and unsubstantiated.
With these arguments, the counsel requested that the court dismiss the petition in its entirety, and sought heavy costs against the petitioner for what they described as frivolous litigation.

17. Upon perusal of the pleadings and documents submitted by both parties, it is an admitted fact that the petitioner has entered into a second marriage with the respondent No.1 and lived together as husband and wife in a shared household following their marriage.
Out of their wedlock, a male child born to them on 12.06.2006.
Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 18.
The entire case fundamentally rests on the evidence provided by Ex.P.8, the birth certificate.
The petitioner places significant reliance on this document, claiming it belongs to the son of the first respondent, born to a woman named Saraswathi.
However, the respondents categorically deny this assertion, leading to a contentious dispute over the implications of the birth certificate.
19. Upon thorough examination of Ex.P.8, it is revealed that the child, H.R. Rohit, was born on March 10, 2015, at City Clinic Hospital.
The birth certificate explicitly lists the mother as Saraswathi and identifies the father as Ramachandra G.
This information is critical as it directly ties the paternity of the child to the name indicated on the certificate.

Additionally, the document provides the addresses of the parents at the time of the child's birth and their permanent address, which is stated as "No. 144, Krishna Layout, Hulimavu, B.G. Road, Bengaluru - 560 076."
This address serves as a key detail in linking the individuals involved to the claims made by the petitioner.
Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 20.

In contrast, the address of the first respondent, as provided in the petition and his evidence affidavit, is listed as "No. 144, Near SLV Bar, Krishna Layout, "Begur Road", Hulimavu, B.G. Road,
Bengaluru - 560 076."
A comparative analysis of these two addresses reveals significant similarities.

The only notable difference is the inclusion of "Begur Road" in the first respondent's address, which Manjula M vs Ramachandra on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93755606/
5 is absent from the birth certificate.

sentences.text: This proximity in addresses raises important questions about the relationship between the first respondent and the information presented in Ex.P.8.
The fact that both addresses share the same house number and locality could imply a connection, potentially supporting the petitioner's claims regarding the first respondent's paternity of the child.
Furthermore, this similarity may lead to implications regarding the credibility of the first respondent's denials.

If the first respondent is indeed the individual identified as the father in the birth certificate, this could substantiate the petitioner's allegations of extramarital relations and subsequent mental cruelty stemming from those actions.
Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 21.
At this juncture, it is pertinent to examine Ex.P.8, the birth certificate.

This document indicates that it was issued by the Chief Registrar of Births and Deaths, specifically under Section 12/17 of the Registration of Births and Deaths (RBD) Act, 1969, as well as Rule 8/13 of the Karnataka Registration of Deaths and Births (KRDB) Rules, 1999.

sentences.text:
The birth certificate also references the original record of birth maintained in the register of the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike,
located in the Bengaluru District of Karnataka State.
22. It is well-established law that entries in the Births and Deaths Registers are considered public documents and are admissible under Section 35 of the Evidence Act.
Consequently, there is no necessity to prove who made the entries or what the source of the information was.
Given that the register is a public document, a presumption of correctness attaches to it, and the burden of proof lies with the party seeking to dispute this presumption.

As such, the birth certificate is admissible as a public document because it was issued based on the records maintained under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 1969.

entities.text: Registration of Births and Deaths Act
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Therefore, no formal proof is required to establish its validity.

Keeping in mind the established legal principle that a birth certificate issued by a competent authority is a public document admissible in evidence, the burden of disproof falls heavily on the opposing party.
In this case, however, there is insufficient material to effectively disprove the contents of Ex.P.8.

Given the absence of a credible challenge to the validity of the birth certificate, this Court is of the opinion that the petitioner has successfully established, by a preponderance of probabilities, that the first respondent has a child named Rohit from an extramarital relationship with a woman named Saraswathi.
23. Moreover, upon careful examination of the cross- examination of PW.1, it is evident that the learned counsel for the respondents conducted thorough questioning of the witness.

However,
notably absent from this cross-examination were any questions or suggestions challenging the validity or genuineness of Ex.P.8, the birth certificate.
This omission is significant; it suggests that the respondents do not contest the authenticity of this document.

Given the lack of any rebuttal Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT regarding the birth certificate during the cross-examination, this Court can reasonably infer that, Ex.P.8 is indeed a genuine document pertaining to the son of the first respondent.
The failure to raise any doubts about the certificate during such a critical phase of the proceedings reinforces its credibility.
The implications of this finding are substantial.
By establishing the authenticity of Ex.P.8, the Court can further substantiate the petitioner's claims regarding the first respondent's extramarital relationship and the resultant child.

This authenticity Manjula M vs Ramachandra on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93755606/
6
not only strengthens the petitioner's case but also raises important questions about the responsibilities and obligations of the first respondent towards his child and the petitioner.
In conclusion, the absence of any challenge to the validity of Ex.P.8 during the cross-examination of PW.1 allows this Court to accept the birth certificate as a credible piece of evidence.
24. The existence of this child, born during the subsistence of the marriage between the petitioner and the first respondent, constitutes mental cruelty.
Such cruelty falls within the definition of domestic violence as outlined in Section Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 3 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.

entities.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The implications of this finding are significant, as they underline the emotional and psychological toll inflicted upon the petitioner due to the first respondent's actions.
Mental cruelty, particularly in the context of an extramarital affair, can manifest in various ways, leading to severe emotional distress for the affected partner.

The acknowledgment of a child born from such a relationship not only breaches the trust that is foundational to a marriage but also exposes the petitioner to feelings of betrayal, humiliation, and isolation.
This betrayal is compounded by societal stigma and the psychological burden of navigating a marital relationship that is fundamentally altered by infidelity.

Under the PWDV Act,
the term "domestic violence"
encompasses not just physical abuse but also emotional and psychological abuse.
The petitioner's experience of mental cruelty aligns with these definitions, illustrating how the first respondent's actions have caused significant emotional harm.
The recognition of this emotional abuse is crucial, as it validates the petitioner's experiences and reinforces her right to seek legal protection and redress.

Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 25. The learned counsel representing the first respondent argued that the petitioner's filing of a divorce petition against him indicates her intention to abandon the marital relationship.

Consequently, it was asserted that she is not entitled to seek relief under the provisions of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.
26.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Upon perusal of Ex.R.3, the copy of the divorce petition, and the cross-examination of PW.1, it is noted that PW.1 admitted during cross-examination that she filed a divorce petition against the first respondent, which was subsequently dismissed for non-prosecution.

However, it is well-established law that a petitioner's eligibility to seek relief under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence (PWDV) Act should be assessed based on her marital status at the time of filing the petition, as well as the specific circumstances surrounding her situation.

entities.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence (PWDV) Act
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The Court emphasizes that the petitioner's rights under the PWDV Act must be evaluated in light of the legal status that existed when she initiated her legal proceedings.
This approach ensures that her access to remedies Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT under domestic violence laws is appropriately determined, regardless of subsequent actions.

sentences.text: In the context of marital relationships, emotional abuse is recognized as a form of domestic violence under Section 3 of the PWDV Act.
This section defines emotional abuse broadly, encompassing any act, omission, or conduct that inflicts mental or emotional harm upon the aggrieved person.
Importantly, emotional abuse does not necessarily involve physical violence; it can profoundly affect a person's psychological well-being and overall quality of life.
In this case, the actions of the first respondent--namely, marrying the petitioner while simultaneously having a child with another woman--can be interpreted as emotional abuse under the PWDV Act.

Such behavior inflicts significant distress and emotional turmoil upon the petitioner,
undermining her mental health and sense of security.
The psychological impact of such betrayal can lead to feelings of inadequacy, isolation, and anxiety, as the petitioner grapples with the reality of her partner's dual commitments.
Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 28.
Furthermore, the first respondent's actions can create a toxic environment within the marriage, characterized by distrust and insecurity.
The emotional fallout from such circumstances can lead to long-term psychological consequences, affecting not only the petitioner's mental state but also her overall quality of life.
It is essential to recognize that emotional abuse can be just as damaging as physical abuse, warranting equal consideration under the law.
Therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that the petitioner has successfully demonstrated that she has been subjected to both cruelty and domestic violence by the first respondent.
The evidence presented supports her claims of emotional abuse and highlights the detrimental effects on her well-being.
Furthermore, it is evident that the first respondent has abandoned and neglected the petitioner, failing to provide any maintenance or support during this period.
This abandonment not only exacerbates the emotional distress but also raises significant concerns regarding the first respondent's responsibilities towards the petitioner.
The cumulative effect of Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT these actions substantiates the petitioner's claims under the PWDV Act, warranting the relief she seeks.
In light of the evidence and the emotional turmoil caused by the first respondent's conduct, it is imperative that the Court recognizes the validity of her claims and provides appropriate remedies.
The recognition of emotional abuse and neglect is crucial in ensuring that the petitioner receives the support and protection she is entitled to under the law.
With these observations, this Court answers the points No.1 and 2 in the AFFIRMATIVE.
29. Point No.3 :
As discussed above, the petitioner has successfully demonstrated that she has been subjected to cruelty and has been deserted by the respondents.
The petitioner has asserted that the first respondent has failed to provide maintenance or arrange suitable accommodation for her and their child.
Furthermore, she contends that the first respondent is engaged in real estate and operates a traveling agency under the name "Bhagavati Tours and Travels."

He is also involved in an automobile agency that deals with the buying and selling of vehicles and reportedly owns two Manjula M vs Ramachandra on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93755606/
8
TATA Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT Sumo vehicles and a goods vehicle.

As such,
the petitioner claims that he has a sufficient source of income exceeding Rs. 1,00,000 per month.
However, she has not produced any documentary evidence to substantiate these claims.

30. In contrast, the first respondent has stated in his affidavit regarding the disclosure of assets and liabilities that he works as a car driver and earns approximately Rs. 15,000 per month and the petitioner operates a business supplying manpower to apartments, earning a substantial income.
She also owns residential properties that generate rental income.
Similar to the petitioner, he has also failed to provide any supporting documents to verify this claim.

31. It is essential to reference our scriptures, which assert the principle that "bharta rakshati yavvane," translating to the idea that it is the husband's duty to provide maintenance to his dependent wife.
This principle is deeply rooted in our cultural heritage and is reflected in the legal frameworks governing marital relationships.
Our legislation explicitly mandates that a husband must provide financial support to his Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT wife, irrespective of her income or financial independence.
This legal obligation underscores the importance of spousal support in maintaining the dignity and welfare of the family unit.
32. In the present case, the evidence clearly indicates that the petitioner and her son have been living separately from Respondent No.1, the husband.

As the spouse,
Respondent No. 1 carries the inherent responsibility of maintaining the petitioner,
especially in light of the marital relationship they share.
The absence of this support has left the petitioner in a precarious position, both financially and emotionally.

The petitioner has made a compelling case for her entitlement to compensation, which is not only a matter of financial assistance but also a means of restoring her dignity and status that have been compromised due to the separation and lack of support.
33. This Court, having thoroughly perusal of the materials presented, recognizes the disparity created by the respondent No.1's failure to provide for the petitioner.
It is clear Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT that the petitioner has been deprived of the lifestyle and support she rightfully deserves as a married woman.

Thus, after careful consideration of the respondent No.1's income and the circumstances surrounding their separation, this Court determines that the petitioner is entitled to compensation or damages amounting to Rs.8,00,000/-.
This figure serves as a reasonable estimate for what is necessary to ensure the petitioner can lead a life comparable to the status and standard of living, she was accustomed to during the marriage.
34. Furthermore, this compensation is not merely a transactional obligation; it represents a commitment to uphold the values of marital responsibility and support.

By ensuring that the petitioner receives this amount, the Court acknowledges the need to rectify the financial and emotional imbalance that has arisen from Manjula M vs Ramachandra on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93755606/
9

sentences.text: Respondent No.1's neglect of his duties.
This decision aims to empower the petitioner to reclaim her independence and security in the face of the challenges posed by her current circumstances.
Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 35.
In conclusion, the Court firmly believes that the maintenance of the petitioner is not only a legal obligation but a moral imperative that reflects the essence of marital partnership.

Therefore, the Court orders that Respondent No. 1 shall pay the petitioner Rs.8,00,000/- in compensation, ensuring that she is adequately supported and can continue her life with the dignity and respect that every individual deserves.
With this observation, this Court answers Point No.3 accordingly.
36. Point No.4 :

In view of discussion held above, this Court proceed to pass the following;
ORDER
The petition filed by the petitioner under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act., is hereby partly allowed.

This document indicates that it was issued by the Chief Registrar of Births and Deaths, specifically under Section 12/17 of the Registration of Births and Deaths (RBD) Act, 1969, as well as Rule 8/13 of the Karnataka Registration of Deaths and Births (KRDB) Rules, 1999.
22. It is well-established law that entries in the Births and Deaths Registers are considered public documents and are admissible under Section 35 of the Evidence Act.
Consequently, there is no necessity to prove who made the entries or what the source of the information was.
Given that the register is a public document, a presumption of correctness attaches to it, and the burden of proof lies with the party seeking to dispute this presumption.
As such, the birth certificate is admissible as a public document because it was issued based on the records maintained under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 1969.
Therefore, no formal proof is required to establish its validity.
Keeping in mind the established legal principle that a birth certificate issued by a competent authority is a public document admissible in evidence, the burden of disproof falls heavily on the opposing party.
In this case, however, there is insufficient material to effectively disprove the contents of Ex.P.8.
Given the absence of a credible challenge to the validity of the birth certificate, this Court is of the opinion that the petitioner has successfully established, by a preponderance of probabilities, that the first respondent has a child named Rohit from an extramarital relationship with a woman named Saraswathi.
Given the lack of any rebuttal Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT regarding the birth certificate during the cross-examination, this Court can reasonably infer that, Ex.P.8 is indeed a genuine document pertaining to the son of the first respondent.
The failure to raise any doubts about the certificate during such a critical phase of the proceedings reinforces its credibility.
By establishing the authenticity of Ex.P.8, the Court can further substantiate the petitioner's claims regarding the first respondent's extramarital relationship and the resultant child.
24. The existence of this child, born during the subsistence of the marriage between the petitioner and the first respondent, constitutes mental cruelty.
Such cruelty falls within the definition of domestic violence as outlined in Section Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT 3 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.
Mental cruelty, particularly in the context of an extramarital affair, can manifest in various ways, leading to severe emotional distress for the affected partner.
The acknowledgment of a child born from such a relationship not only breaches the trust that is foundational to a marriage but also exposes the petitioner to feelings of betrayal, humiliation, and isolation.
This betrayal is compounded by societal stigma and the psychological burden of navigating a marital relationship that is fundamentally altered by infidelity.
Under the PWDV Act,
the term "domestic violence"
encompasses not just physical abuse but also emotional and psychological abuse.
In this case, the actions of the first respondent--namely, marrying the petitioner while simultaneously having a child with another woman--can be interpreted as emotional abuse under the PWDV Act.
Such behavior inflicts significant distress and emotional turmoil upon the petitioner,
undermining her mental health and sense of security.
The psychological impact of such betrayal can lead to feelings of inadequacy, isolation, and anxiety, as the petitioner grapples with the reality of her partner's dual commitments.
Furthermore, the first respondent's actions can create a toxic environment within the marriage, characterized by distrust and insecurity.
The emotional fallout from such circumstances can lead to long-term psychological consequences, affecting not only the petitioner's mental state but also her overall quality of life.
It is essential to recognize that emotional abuse can be just as damaging as physical abuse, warranting equal consideration under the law.
The recognition of emotional abuse and neglect is crucial in ensuring that the petitioner receives the support and protection she is entitled to under the law.
Our legislation explicitly mandates that a husband must provide financial support to his Crl.Mis.No.113/2017 JUDGMENT wife, irrespective of her income or financial independence.
This legal obligation underscores the importance of spousal support in maintaining the dignity and welfare of the family unit.
32. In the present case, the evidence clearly indicates that the petitioner and her son have been living separately from Respondent No.1, the husband.
As the spouse,
Respondent No. 1 carries the inherent responsibility of maintaining the petitioner,
especially in light of the marital relationship they share.
